before: Look at the bottom of this page before you turn it. There are two marks down there, and they are not decoration. One is a solid slab carrying the page number. The other is an outline of the same shape, and it carries nothing at all.
after: An observation is a record of an event. An inference suggests what it means. A measurement adds a quantity, a unit and an estimate of uncertainty. Keep these distinct when you read a claim.

before: Read them as a pair and they are the whole method. The solid one is what has been settled — measured, checked, written down, and now countable. The empty one is the same shape waiting to be filled: the question not yet answered, which is the larger half of science and always will be. Both run off the edge of the paper rather than stopping neatly at the margin, because neither the evidence nor the questions end where this book does.
after: Suppose a plant beside a window is taller than one across the room. The height difference is an observation; saying that light caused it is an inference. Different watering or starting sizes could also explain it. A comparison needs to account for those alternatives.

before: Boxes with a rule above and below are asides: a thread of curiosity to follow, or a note. Boxes with a tinted ground are matter to work through — an example, a question put to you, or a step past the syllabus. None of them is optional reading; they are simply doing different jobs.
after: Throughout this book, teal marks first-hand work, amber marks questions to think through, and brown marks evidence or mechanisms. Record your work in your notebook. Judge each conclusion by the observations supporting it.

before: What the foot of the page is telling you
after: Separating evidence from explanation

before: Notice that a model is not really true or false. It is useful, or it is not, and only for a stated purpose. The same car is a point when you ask where it will be in ten seconds, a set of springs when you ask why the ride is bumpy, and a rectangle two and a half metres long when you ask whether it will fit in the parking space. All three are the same car and all three are correct.
after: Models make claims that can agree or disagree with evidence. Their usefulness depends on the purpose and accuracy required; calling something a model does not exempt it from testing.

before: Three things have to be in it: how fast the ball left the bat, the direction it left in, and gravity pulling it down all the way. With those three you can work out the whole flight.
after: A first model needs launch speed, launch direction, launch height and gravitational acceleration. It also needs the boundary distance and landing level to answer the question. Treat the ball as a point and neglect air resistance initially.

before: And three things sit in between — the air pushing back, the spin the ball carries, the stitching at the seam. These are real, and they do change the answer a little. We leave them out of a first model knowing that we are doing it, and put them back if the first answer turns out not to be good enough.
after: Air resistance, spin and the seam can substantially affect a ball's path. Whether ignoring them is acceptable depends on the accuracy needed, especially near the boundary. Compare the model with measurements.

before: The whole flight follows from three quantities.
after: This first model requires launch conditions, gravity and the relevant distances.

before: Everything written below the ground line is true of the ball and makes no difference to the question.
after: Compare omitted effects with the accuracy needed before deciding that they do not matter.

before: holding a heavy bag perfectly still is no work at all
after: holding a bag still does no mechanical work on the bag, though your muscles use energy

before: the candela for the brightness of a light
after: the candela for luminous intensity in a specified direction

before: One system, and only seven units in it
after: One system with seven base units

before: a thermometer compares a warmth with the kelvin
after: a thermometer measures temperature on a defined scale

before: Newton's laws of motion are laws in exactly that sense. They tell you that a bus braking sharply will throw a standing passenger forwards, and by how much, without saying a word about why matter behaves that way. Atomic theory is a theory: it explains why elements combine in fixed ratios, why a compound has properties neither of its parts had, and why a chemical equation balances — three facts that look unrelated until the theory joins them. Conservation of energy is a principle: you can apply it to a falling stone, a boiling kettle or a climbing child without needing a separate law for each.
after: Newton's laws explain the motion of a passenger relative to a braking bus: without a sufficient backward force, the passenger continues forwards while the bus slows. The passenger is not thrown forwards by a new forward force.

before: These are not guesses dressed up. A guess cannot be wrong in any useful way — it is just a preference. A prediction commits you: it names an outcome, in advance, precisely enough that the world can contradict it. That exposure is the whole point.
after: A prediction specifies an expected observation before the test, clearly enough to compare it with a result. It may follow from a model or a tentative explanation. A prediction can be qualitative or numerical.

before: Notice which arrow does the work. When a prediction comes true, very little happens: the model was already good enough and stays as it was. It is the return arrow — the day the measurement disagrees — that forces somebody to look again at the model, the assumptions, or the instrument, and that is where new science comes from.
after: Both outcomes matter. Agreement supports a model within the tested conditions, though alternatives may fit too. Disagreement prompts checks of observations, assumptions and calculations. Neither outcome alone settles the whole theory.

before: The loop only closes when a prediction fails.
after: The loop includes both agreement and disagreement with observations.

before: The claim is not wrong — it may well rain. The trouble is that it cannot fail in any particular way, so nothing is learnt whether it rains or not. Useful questions ask for numbers and for what happened last time.
after: “It will rain this afternoon” is already testable if the place, time interval and meaning of rain are clear. Dark clouds are a proposed reason, whose reliability needs separate checks. A yes-or-no prediction can fail.

before: Each of those can be answered with a measurement and compared with a record, and together they turn an impression into a prediction that the afternoon can settle. Questions with a plain yes or no — do you think it will rain? — do not.
after: Measurements and past records help assess whether dark clouds predict rain reliably. Define a location, an interval such as noon to 6 p.m., and a detectable amount of rain. Record both rainy and dry afternoons, including cases where the prediction failed.

before: The difficulty is of a different kind. The atmosphere is arranged so that two states almost identical today can be quite different in a week. A tiny error in today's measurement — and every measurement has one — grows as the model runs forward, until at some point the forecast carries no information at all.
after: Small differences in initial atmospheric conditions can grow as a model runs forward. Forecasters use sets of model runs to explore uncertainty. Model limitations and incomplete observations also contribute to error.

before: That is why a forecast for this evening is worth acting on, one for next weekend is worth glancing at, and one for a date next month could not be made reliable by any amount of computing power. The limit is in the weather, not in the forecaster.
after: Forecast uncertainty usually grows with lead time. A detailed forecast for one place on one day differs from a probabilistic outlook for average conditions over a month. Computing, measurements and models all affect skill; there is no single time limit for every forecast question.

before: So ask: by what mechanism? What reaches the food that did not reach it an hour earlier? What chemical change is being proposed, and why does the same food keep perfectly well in the shade of a tree, or indoors at night, when the shadow is far deeper and lasts far longer? No answer survives being asked, which is how you know.
after: Ask what change to food is proposed and what evidence would distinguish it from ordinary spoilage. An eclipse blocks sunlight; it does not introduce a special food-poisoning radiation. Food still needs normal hygiene and safe storage. Absence of a proposed mechanism alone would not disprove a measured effect.

before: Everyone outside that patch sees an ordinary day.
after: Outside the path of totality, a wider region sees a partial eclipse; beyond that region there is no eclipse.

before: Nothing else about that patch changes.
after: Reduced sunlight can also affect temperature and animal behaviour.

before: This one is for deciding what size of sack to buy.
after: This one estimates an energy equivalent, not a real family's shopping requirement.

before: The volume of one breath is harder, so find something to compare it with. A party balloon holds about 2 litres and takes four or five breaths to inflate, so one quiet breath is around half a litre.
after: For a resting adult, use half a litre as an approximate quiet-breath volume. Do not infer it from blowing up a balloon: those breaths are usually deeper than normal breathing. The estimate varies with body size and activity.

before: Is that believable? Check it another way. If you could blow up three balloons a minute, that would be $3 \times 2 = 6$ litres a minute, or about 8600 litres in a day — the same answer to within a fifth, reached from a different direction. Two rough routes agreeing is worth more than one exact-looking number.
after: The same assumptions give about 7.5 litres per minute. Multiplying by 1440 minutes checks the arithmetic but is not independent evidence: it reuses the same breathing rate and volume. An independent check would need different measurements.

before: Turn back to the foot of the first page if you like. The solid mark and the empty one are down there on every leaf of this book, and the empty one is much the larger of the two. Go and fill some of it in.
after: Choose one claim in this chapter. State the evidence for it, an alternative explanation and an observation that would help distinguish them.

before: A model is not true or false but useful or useless
after: A model must be tested against evidence

before: In science a theory is a conclusion, not a guess.
after: A scientific theory is a tested explanatory framework, not a promotion stage between a hypothesis and a law.

before: A prediction is worth more than an explanation offered afterwards, because it can fail. The useful arrow in the cycle is the one that runs back from a failed test.
after: A prediction can be checked against an observation. Both agreement and disagreement provide evidence; neither alone proves or disproves every aspect of a model.
